power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .519", "p = .351"), Sentence = c("Second, multiple regression indicated that weekly duration-pattern inconsistency, measured using seven-day root mean square successive differences (RMSSD), was not significantly associated with average meaning in life, b = -0.159, p = .519, R² = .011.", "Third, within-person standard deviations in daily religious duration were also unrelated to average meaning in life, b = 0.263, p = .351, R² = .019." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

info.title: Religious Behavior Duration, Perceived Value, and Daily Meaning in Life: A 50-Day Diary Study Using Residual Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling

									1001 84660
									UT

text.text: Religious engagement has been associated with meaning in life, yet research has primarily examined how much people engage in religious behaviors rather than how valuable they perceive those behaviors to be.
Drawing on values theory and situated expectancy-value theory, we examined whether religious behavior duration and perceived behavioral value show distinct associations with daily meaning in life.
Participants completed daily surveys over 50 days, reporting time spent across 16 religious activities, perceived value of activities performed, and meaning in life.
The analytic sample included 90 adults.

Using Bayesian residual dynamic structural equation modeling (RDSEM), we separated withinperson fluctuations from between-person differences and accounted for temporal dependencies and systematic weekend effects.

In an exploratory joint model, both longer-than-usual religious behavior duration (β = .11, 95% credible interval [.056, .16]) and greater-than-usual perceived value (β = .19, 95% credible interval [.15, .23]) were independently associated with greater same-day meaning in life.
Between individuals, average perceived value was associated with greater meaning in life (β = .53), whereas average duration was not.

Preregistered analyses found no credible association between consistency of religious engagement and meaning, no average reciprocal next-day associations between duration and value, and no evidence that perceived value moderated the duration-meaning association.
Additional exploratory analyses revealed no consistent next-day associations with meaning in life.

Findings suggest that time spent engaging in religion and the value attributed to those experiences are distinct correlates of daily meaning, highlighting the importance of assessing perceived behavioral value alongside duration.
Studying outcomes of behaviors is a common, and important part of most research programs within the social sciences.

This can be done by focusing on the outcomes associated with how much, or how long people may engage with a particular behavior, but this ignores the effect of how individuals subjectively experience or value those behaviors.
Through two theoretical perspectives, we suggest that the perceived value of a behavior may also influence its outcomes.
Individuals may perceive a behavior as valuable for several reasons.

Behaviors may be perceived as valuable because they are enjoyable, instantiate abstract values, help attain valued goals, or feel important to one's identity (Eccles & Wigfield, 2024; Hanel et al., 2018; Maio, 2010).
text.formatted: Behaviors may be perceived as valuable because they are enjoyable, instantiate abstract values, help attain valued goals, or feel important to one's identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Hanel et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Maio, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Valued behaviors should be more motivating and more likely to be repeated, though whether that process is adaptive intuitively depends on the behavior itself.
Engagement in valued behaviors may be especially important to developing meaning in life by connecting behavior with valued principles and goals (Caldaroni et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Engagement in valued behaviors may be especially important to developing meaning in life by connecting behavior with valued principles and goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Caldaroni et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Religion provides a relevant developmental context for examining these relationships, given the established associations between religious behavior and meaning in life (Prinzing et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Religion provides a relevant developmental context for examining these relationships, given the established associations between religious behavior and meaning in life <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Prinzing et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, the present study uses intensive longitudinal data and residual dynamic structural equation modeling (RDSEM) to examine how both the duration and perceived value of religious behaviors relate to daily meaning in life.
There are multiple theories we can draw on when making claims about the importance of studying perceived behavioral value, particularly for domain-specific activities such as religious behaviors.
One line of reasoning builds upon values literature while the other follows the situated expectancy-value model literature.
Both theories may predict adaptive outcomes, such as meaning in life, depending on the behavior of study.
Regarding values theory, values are abstract guiding principles that shape what individuals consider desirable and may motivate corresponding behaviors (Maio, 2010; Rokeach, 1973; Schwartz, 1992).
text.formatted: Regarding values theory, values are abstract guiding principles that shape what individuals consider desirable and may motivate corresponding behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Maio, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Rokeach, 1973;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Schwartz, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Values are distinct from more proximal and concrete predictors of behaviors such as attitudes, intentions, and goals (Ajzen & Fishbein, 2005). Maio (2010) conceptualized three levels to values theory: systems (relationships between values), values (such as obedience), and value instantiations-the behaviors expressing those values.
text.formatted: Values are distinct from more proximal and concrete predictors of behaviors such as attitudes, intentions, and goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ajzen & Fishbein, 2005)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Maio (2010)</ref> conceptualized three levels to values theory: systems (relationships between values), values (such as obedience), and value instantiations-the behaviors expressing those values.

text.text: Because values are abstract, the same behavior may instantiate different abstract and possibly related values, which can make a behavior feel valuable (Hanel et al., 2018; Maio, 2010).
text.formatted: Because values are abstract, the same behavior may instantiate different abstract and possibly related values, which can make a behavior feel valuable <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Hanel et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Maio, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: For example, prayer may express conservation, self-enhancement, openness to change, self-transcendence, or some combination of these four higher-order value domains identified by Schwartz (1992).
text.formatted: For example, prayer may express conservation, self-enhancement, openness to change, self-transcendence, or some combination of these four higher-order value domains identified by <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Schwartz (1992)</ref>.

text.text: One reason individuals may perceive a behavior as valuable is that it instantiates personally important abstract values.
Thus, value instantiation provides one theoretical rationale for studying perceived behavioral value alongside behavioral engagement.

Furthermore, values may motivate corresponding behaviors, while repeated engagement may reinforce or alter certain values (Bardi et al., 2009; Maio, 2010), suggesting potential bidirectional influences between behavioral engagement and perceived behavioral value.
text.formatted: Furthermore, values may motivate corresponding behaviors, while repeated engagement may reinforce or alter certain values <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bardi et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Maio, 2010)</ref>, suggesting potential bidirectional influences between behavioral engagement and perceived behavioral value.

text.text: Thus, beyond duration, the perceived value of religious behaviors may reflect the extent to which individuals experience them as expressions of personally important values, making them valued behaviors.
A second explanation justifying the importance of studying valued behaviors extends beyond values to the subjective experience of the activity itself.

Situated expectancy-value theory conceptualizes this as subjective task value, comprising intrinsic value (enjoyment), utility value (usefulness for achieving goals), attainment value (personal importance), and perceived cost (Eccles & Wigfield, 2024).
text.formatted: Situated expectancy-value theory conceptualizes this as subjective task value, comprising intrinsic value (enjoyment), utility value (usefulness for achieving goals), attainment value (personal importance), and perceived cost <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, a single behavior being seen as valuable may involve multiple components.
For example, attending a worship service may be enjoyable, help fulfill a religious goal, satisfy a need for belonging, and may do this with a relatively low perceived cost.

Together, these two theoretical perspectives suggest that religious behaviors may be perceived as valuable for multiple reasons: they may instantiate abstract values, fulfill social expectations, reflect prior reinforcement, provide intrinsic enjoyment, help achieve desired outcomes, or hold personal importance.
Thus, perceived behavioral value may capture dimensions of meaningful behavior engagement beyond what behavioral duration can.
In addition to justifying perceived behavioral value as a construct of interest, value instantiation and subjective task value offer another contribution to the present study.
They both present complementary explanations for how perceived behavioral value may motivate engagement.
This demonstrates a theoretical link between perceived behavioral value and later behavioral engagement.

Behaviors expressing abstract values may encourage value-consistent action (Hanel et al., 2018; Maio, 2010), while those perceived as enjoyable, useful, or personally important may motivate repeated engagement (Eccles & Wigfield, 2024).
text.formatted: Behaviors expressing abstract values may encourage value-consistent action <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Hanel et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Maio, 2010)</ref>, while those perceived as enjoyable, useful, or personally important may motivate repeated engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, engaging in valued behaviors may lead to repeating those behaviors.
However, whether such engagement promotes adaptive outcomes, however, likely depends on the nature of the valued behavior.
But in general, it appears that engaging in valued behaviors may provide experiences through which individuals develop a stronger sense of meaning in life (Caldaroni et al., 2026).
text.formatted: But in general, it appears that engaging in valued behaviors may provide experiences through which individuals develop a stronger sense of meaning in life <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Caldaroni et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, examining both the duration of religious behaviors and their perceived value may capture complementary dimensions of behavioral engagement predicting meaning in life and help explain why the same behaviors have different outcomes across individuals.
One potential outcome of engaging in valued behaviors is a greater sense of meaning in life.

Before examining this relationship, it is important to distinguish between two related constructs. Fuhrer et al., (2026) differentiate between believing that life has inherent meaning (meaning of life) and experiencing one's own life as meaningful (meaning in life).

text.text: Additionally, Fuhrer et al. (2026) note that for much of prior quantitative research, the phenomenon that has been studied has actually been meaning in life, even if the claim has been meaning of life.

text.text: Therefore, although meaning of life appears more theoretically tied to religious and metaphysical beliefs, meaning in life is the construct that has historically been linked to well-being, health, and longevity (Fuhrer et al., 2026; Routledge & FioRito, 2021).

text.text: Accordingly, we build on this literature by examining whether religious engagement predicts the extent to which individuals experience their own lives as meaningful.
Understanding how meaning in life develops is particularly important given its relevance to human development and well-being.
Experiencing meaning in life may be an evolutionarily adaptive outcome that contributes to self-actualization (Upenieks, 2022).
text.formatted: Experiencing meaning in life may be an evolutionarily adaptive outcome that contributes to self-actualization <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Upenieks, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Meaning in life has also been associated with longer, healthier lives and has been found to uniquely predict health-related behaviors, such as physical activity, beyond other measures of well-being (Routledge & FioRito, 2021).
text.formatted: Meaning in life has also been associated with longer, healthier lives and has been found to uniquely predict health-related behaviors, such as physical activity, beyond other measures of well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Routledge & FioRito, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These findings support the notion that meaning in life is an essential human need that deserves greater attention to how it can be predicted both within and between people.
Knowing that meaning in life is an important developmental outcome, common places meaning in life can develop is via systems and routines.

Individuals find meaning in life through diverse systems, including family, relationships, employment, education, recreational activities, and religious faith ("Where Americans Find Meaning in Life," 2018).
Beyond systems, routines of behaviors may also contribute to the development of meaning in life.

Behavioral routines are best conceptualized as recurring patterns of behavior, and have shown to influence meaning in life by providing structure and coherence to everyday experiences (Heintzelman & King, 2019; Mohideen & Heintzelman, 2023).
text.formatted: Behavioral routines are best conceptualized as recurring patterns of behavior, and have shown to influence meaning in life by providing structure and coherence to everyday experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Heintzelman & King, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Mohideen & Heintzelman, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Religion provides a relevant developmental context for studying meaning in life, particularly in the United States, where more than half of adults identify with a religious tradition (Smith et al., 2025).

text.text: In general, research shows that religion may help fulfill fundamental needs by shaping worldviews (Greenberg et al., 2014), fostering belonging (Baumeister & Leary, 1995), and supporting well-being (Hinkel et al., 2021; Koçak, 2022).
text.formatted: In general, research shows that religion may help fulfill fundamental needs by shaping worldviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Greenberg et al., 2014)</ref>, fostering belonging <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baumeister & Leary, 1995)</ref>, and supporting well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Hinkel et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Koçak, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Particularly relevant to the present study, religion may also predict meaning in life (Prinzing et al., 2023), which has been found to mediate the association between religiousness and well-being (Steger & Frazier, 2005).

text.text: Religious behaviors, broadly defined as activities undertaken for religious purposes, may provide one pathway through which individuals develop meaning in life.

Research has generally found positive associations between both public and private religious behaviors and meaning in life (Fuhrer et al., 2026; Prinzing et al., 2023), with consistent or increasing religious behavioral engagement also associated with greater meaning in life (Upenieks, 2022).

text.text: Beyond these associations between individuals, research has also examined whether people experience greater meaning in life on days when they engage in more religious activity than usual.
In a 14-day daily-diary study, Steger & Frazier (2005) found that individuals reported greater meaning in life on days with more religious activity relative to their typical levels.

text.text: Similarly, experience-sampling studies found heightened momentary meaning during religious and spiritual practices, including prayer and worship (Choi et al., 2017; Kucinskas et al., 2018). (2023) further identified within-and between-person associations, with positive relationships between religiousness and meaning in life across nightly assessments over 11 weeks and quarterly assessments over 18 months.

(2023)</ref> further identified within-and between-person associations, with positive relationships between religiousness and meaning in life across nightly assessments over 11 weeks and quarterly assessments over 18 months.

text.text: However, their nightly measure assessed religious experience ("I felt God's presence"), while their quarterly measure combined behavioral duration with religious importance.
Thus, although these findings suggest that religious engagement is associated with meaning in life across timescales in general, they do not consider valued behaviors in their assessments.
The present study extends existing research on religious engagement and meaning in life by examining not only the duration of religious behaviors but also their perceived value.
Meaning in life is an important developmental outcome that individuals may cultivate through within various developmental contexts, including religion.

Previous research has established positive associations between religious engagement and meaning in life (Upenieks, 2022), although studies have historically only examined individual behaviors, their duration, or broader measures of religiousness (Prinzing et al., 2023).

text.text: Beyond the amount of engagement, research on behavioral routines suggests that consistent engagement may also contribute to meaning in life (Mohideen & Heintzelman, 2023).

text.text: However, behavioral duration alone is likely not the only path towards meaning in life.

Drawing from values theory and situated expectancy-value theory, behaviors that are perceived as valuable may also contribute to meaning in life development and maintenance (Eccles & Wigfield, 2024; Hanel et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Drawing from values theory and situated expectancy-value theory, behaviors that are perceived as valuable may also contribute to meaning in life development and maintenance <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Hanel et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, perceived value may motivate repeated engagement, while engagement may reinforce perceived value, suggesting potentially bidirectional longitudinal relationships (Bardi et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Furthermore, perceived value may motivate repeated engagement, while engagement may reinforce perceived value, suggesting potentially bidirectional longitudinal relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bardi et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, because behaviors may be valued for different reasons, their perceived value may also influence the association between behavioral duration and meaning in life.
By examining these dimensions separately and together, the present study seeks to clarify how religious behavioral engagement relates to meaning in life.
Although intensive longitudinal studies have found within-person associations between religiousness and meaning in life, modeling these dynamic processes presents methodological challenges.

Combining multilevel and time-series approaches can introduce Lüdtke's bias, arising from measurement error in observed person means, and Nickell's bias, arising when lagged outcomes are associated with stable person-level effects, violating exogeneity assumptions (Gistelinck et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Combining multilevel and time-series approaches can introduce Lüdtke's bias, arising from measurement error in observed person means, and Nickell's bias, arising when lagged outcomes are associated with stable person-level effects, violating exogeneity assumptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Gistelinck et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) helps address these concerns by integrating multilevel, time-series, and structural equation modeling.
Specifically, DSEM uses latent decomposition to distinguish stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations while accounting for temporal dependencies.

Furthermore, residual DSEM (RDSEM) allows researchers to account for systematic weekend effects common to many Judeo-Christian religious practices, reducing potential violations of stationarity and bias in temporal estimates.
This approach allows simultaneous examination of individual differences, within-person associations, and autoregressive effects, making it well suited to the present study.
The study addressed the following preregistered hypotheses: 1.
On days when individuals engage in more religious behavior than usual, they will report greater meaning in life.
On days when individuals perceive their religious behaviors as more valuable than usual, they will report greater meaning in life.
Individuals with less day-to-day variability in religious behavioral duration will report greater meaning in life.
Religious behavioral duration and perceived value will positively predict one another across consecutive days.

Perceived behavioral value will positively moderate the within-person association between religious behavioral duration and meaning in life, such that the association is stronger on days when behaviors are perceived as more valuable.
Duration of Religious Behaviors.

Daily religious behavior duration (or simply duration) was assessed using 16 items corresponding to common religious and spiritual activities, including worship attendance, scripture study, prayer, religious discussion, spiritual reflection, religious music, and participation in religious ordinances (see Table S1 in the online supplements for the full measure).
text.formatted: Daily religious behavior duration (or simply duration) was assessed using 16 items corresponding to common religious and spiritual activities, including worship attendance, scripture study, prayer, religious discussion, spiritual reflection, religious music, and participation in religious ordinances (see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref> in the online supplements for the full measure).

text.text: For each activity, participants reported the approximate number of minutes spent engaging in that activity that day.
Minutes were summed across available activity responses and converted to hours by dividing by 60.
Missing activity-level responses were excluded from the daily sum; daily duration was coded as missing when all 16 activity responses were missing.
Perceived Religious Behavioral Value.

The perceived value of religious behaviors engaged in during daily life (or simply value) was assessed using 16 items corresponding to common religious and spiritual activities, including worship attendance, scripture study, prayer, religious discussion, spiritual reflection, religious music, and participation in religious ordinances (see Table S2 in the online supplements for the full measure).
text.formatted: The perceived value of religious behaviors engaged in during daily life (or simply value) was assessed using 16 items corresponding to common religious and spiritual activities, including worship attendance, scripture study, prayer, religious discussion, spiritual reflection, religious music, and participation in religious ordinances (see Table <ref type="table">S2</ref> in the online supplements for the full measure).

text.text: For each activity completed that day, participants rated the average value, significance, or impact of their time spent in that activity using a scale from 0 (not at all valuable) to 10 (extremely valuable).
Ratings were averaged across available activities to indicate the average value of religious behaviors for that day.
Daily value was coded as missing when no value ratings were available.
Daily meaning in life was assessed using three items capturing adolescents' sense of meaning, purpose, and significance in life that day (see Table S3 in the online supplements for the full measure).

text.text: Participants responded to each item on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 10 (extremely).
A day variable was created from each participant's survey start date and indexed the sequence of daily assessments across the study period.
A weekend dummy variable was then created from the day variable to account for recurring calendar effects.
Including weekend allowed the DSEM to account for systematic weekday-weekend differences while estimating dynamic relations among the residual processes.
Participants were 139 individuals (82% women; 80% European American, 9% African American, 7% Latino, 2% Asian American, and 2% other) ages 18 -69 (M age 25.11, SD 10.77).
Most participants were college students, with 44% enrolled in public universities, 43% in private universities, and 13% not currently enrolled at a university.
By religious affiliation, 24% were Catholic, 22% were Protestant, 37% were Latter-day Saint (LDS or Mormon), 6% were identified with other affiliations, and 11% were not affiliated with any religion.
Regarding marital status, 28% were married.
In terms of education level, 6% had already graduated from a 4-year college or university, while 9% had some education beyond a 4-year degree.
Demographics information is summarized in Table S4 located within the online supplements.

text.text: Participants were recruited from four U.S. universities: two private institutions in the West and Midwest and two public institutions in the East and South.
Institutional review board approval was obtained at each university.
Recruitment occurred through psychology department subject pools and posted flyers.

Interested individuals completed online consent and provided their contact information before receiving an emailed baseline survey through Qualtrics, which assessed demographics and trait-level characteristics.
Several days later, participants began receiving daily surveys for 50 consecutive days.
This period was selected to capture a substantial portion of the academic semester and provide sufficient observations for longitudinal analyses.
Identical survey links were emailed each evening and remained active for 24 hours.
Participants could respond that evening or the following morning or afternoon, but all questions referred to experiences on the day the survey was distributed.
Participants enrolled in psychology courses received extra credit for completing the baseline survey.
Daily survey compensation increased with participation: $1 per survey for the first 20 completed, $2 for the next 20, and $3 for the final 10, allowing participants to earn up to $90.
Additionally, ten $100 Amazon gift cards were awarded through a raffle, with participants receiving one entry for every ten completed daily surveys.
The initial sample included 142 participants.
Thirty-one person-day observations containing no responses to variables of interest were excluded.
Of the remaining 8,822 possible person-day observations, 5,497 were completed (62.3%) and 3,325 were missed (37.7%).
Although compliance was below the ideal 70%-85% reported in reviews of intensive longitudinal studies, missingness is common in such designs (Jones et al., 2019; May et al., 2018; Wen et al., 2017).

Weekend Effect.
Preliminary analyses indicated that several series exhibited systematic temporal trends that violated the assumption of stationarity, partly due to increased weekend religious activity.

Following recommended practice, we addressed this issue using residual DSEM (RDSEM), including a weekend dummy variable to account for recurring calendar effects before estimating the dynamic processes of interest (Figures 1, 3, 4, & 5).

text.text: Thus, the autoregressive and cross-lagged relations were estimated from the detrended residual series rather than the raw observed scores.
Some person-day observations showed unusually high levels of religious behavior duration, often occurring on weekends but varying across weekends.

This pattern likely reflected overlap between the study period and general conference among CJCLDS participants, during which members engage in extended religious instruction that temporarily increases religious behavior engagement.
These calendar-related effects were accounted for in the primary analyses.
Between-person dimensionality was assessed using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) of person-level item averages.
Religious behavior duration did not exhibit a unidimensional reflective structure, supporting its treatment as a cumulative behavioral index.
In contrast, perceived behavioral value and meaning in life exhibited strong standardized factor loadings (.67-.88 and .95-.99, respectively), supporting their composite scores.
Between-person reliability, assessed using Cronbach's alpha, was acceptable for duration (α = .78) and excellent for value (α = .94) and meaning in life (α = .98).
At the within-person level, we decomposed daily scores into latent within-person fluctuations and stable betweenperson differences.
Within-person reliability was assessed using a measurement error autoregressive (MEAR) model (Schuurman & Hamaker, 2019).

All models were estimated using Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, beginning with 1,500 iterations and doubling the number of iterations to assess convergence.
Convergence was evaluated using the potential scale reduction (PSR) statistic, which compares between-chain and within-chain variability.
Values approaching 1.00 (typically ≤ 1.05) were considered indicative of adequate convergence.
We also examined whether PSR values increased with additional iterations.

text.text: Greater daily religious behavior duration was positively associated with daily meaning in life (β = .163, 95% CrI [.094, .219]), explaining approximately 13.1% of within-person variance.
This association varied across individuals.
In a supplementary betweenperson analysis, average religious behavior duration was not credibly associated with average meaning in life (β = .153, 95% CrI [-.073, .370]).
Thus, the hypothesized association was supported within individuals across days, but not between individuals.
Our second hypothesis examined whether individuals reported greater meaning in life on days when they valued their religious behaviors more than usual (Figure 2).

text.text: Greater daily religious behavior value was positively associated with daily meaning in life (β = .227, 95% CrI [.182, .271]), explaining 12.5% of within-person variance.

At the between-person level, average religious behavior value was also positively associated with average meaning in life (β = .516, 95% CrI [.329, .664]), explaining 26.6% of between-person variance.
Thus, perceived value was associated with meaning in life both within and between individuals.
To test our third hypothesis, we examined whether variability in religious behavior duration predicted average meaning in life using three complementary approaches.
First, RDSEM indicated no credible association between residual variability in daily religious duration and average meaning in life (Table 3; Figure 3).

text.text: This measure captured fluctuations unexplained by weekend effects and previous-day duration.

Second, multiple regression indicated that weekly duration-pattern inconsistency, measured using seven-day root mean square successive differences (RMSSD), was not significantly associated with average meaning in life, b = -0.159, p = .519, R² = .011.
Third, within-person standard deviations in daily religious duration were also unrelated to average meaning in life, b = 0.263, p = .351, R² = .019.
Both regressions were done in Stata version 19.5 and controlled for average religious duration.
Thus, none of the three approaches provided evidence that variability in religious behavior duration was associated with average meaning in life.

Results indicated that both duration and value were positively associated with each other, as well as daily meaning at the within-person level, even after accounting for one another (Table 6).

The present study examined how religious behavior duration and perceived value relate to meaning in life, whether consistency in engagement matters, whether duration and value predict one another across days, and whether perceived value moderates or independently contributes to the duration-meaning relationship.
Overall, both duration and perceived value were independently associated with greater daily meaning in life, although only perceived value was associated with meaning across individuals.

We found no evidence that behavioral consistency was associated with meaning, that duration and value predicted one another across days, or that perceived value moderated the duration-meaning relationship.
Our first analysis found that religious behavior duration was positively associated with meaning in life within individuals across days, but not between individuals.

Specifically, participants reported greater meaning in life on days when they engaged in religious behaviors longer than usual, whereas individuals who spent more time engaging in religion on average did not report reliably greater meaning in life (Figure 1, Table 1).

text.text: The within-person finding aligns with previous daily-diary and experience-sampling research linking religious activities to greater daily or momentary meaning (Choi et al., 2017; Steger & Frazier, 2005).

text.text: However, the absence of a credible between-person association differs from previous research identifying positive associations between religiousness and meaning in life across individuals (Prinzing et al., 2023).

text.text: Importantly, previous studies primarily assessed whether individuals engaged in select religious behaviors, such as prayer and worship attendance (Choi et al., 2017; Kucinskas et al., 2018; Prinzing et al., 2023; Steger & Frazier, 2005), rather than how long they spent engaging in a broader range of religious activities.

text.text: Thus, our findings extend previous research by suggesting that the duration of religious engagement may be more consistently associated with daily fluctuations in meaning than with stable differences in meaning across individuals.
Our second analysis suggests that perceiving religious behaviors as more valuable associates with meaning in life.
This is true for both individuals across days, and across people.

Specifically, when a person feels they have greater value in their religious engagement, they may also report feeling greater meaning in life that same day, but also that on average people who engage in valued religious behaviors more may also report greater meaning in life (Figure 2, Table 2).
text.formatted: Specifically, when a person feels they have greater value in their religious engagement, they may also report feeling greater meaning in life that same day, but also that on average people who engage in valued religious behaviors more may also report greater meaning in life (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>, Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Consistent with values theory and situated expectancy-value theory, these findings provide preliminary evidence that engaging in valued behaviors may be relevant to the development and maintenance of meaning in life, potentially extending beyond religious contexts (Eccles & Wigfield, 2024; Hanel et al., 2018).

text.text: Our third analysis found no evidence that consistency in religious behavior duration was associated with meaning in life.
Specifically, individuals who spent more consistent amounts of time engaging in religious behaviors across days or weeks did not report reliably greater meaning in life (Figure 3, Table 3).
text.formatted: Specifically, individuals who spent more consistent amounts of time engaging in religious behaviors across days or weeks did not report reliably greater meaning in life (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">3</ref>, Table <ref type="table">3</ref>).

text.text: This finding contrasts with previous research linking behavioral routines to meaning in life (Mohideen & Heintzelman, 2023).
text.formatted: This finding contrasts with previous research linking behavioral routines to meaning in life <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Mohideen & Heintzelman, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, whereas previous research examined routines as recurring patterns of specific activities, the present study assessed consistency in the total duration of religious engagement.
Thus, consistency in time spent engaging in religion may not capture the structured behavioral routines previously associated with meaning in life.
Our fourth analysis found no credible average cross-lagged associations between religious behavior duration and perceived value.

Specifically, spending more time engaging in religion than usual does not appear to predict greater perceived value the following day, nor do perceiving religious behaviors as more valuable predict greater next-day engagement (Figure 4, Table 4).
text.formatted: Specifically, spending more time engaging in religion than usual does not appear to predict greater perceived value the following day, nor do perceiving religious behaviors as more valuable predict greater next-day engagement (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">4</ref>, Table <ref type="table">4</ref>).

text.text: This was unexpected given values theory and situated expectancy-value theory, which suggest that engaging in valued behaviors may motivate subsequent engagement (Eccles & Wigfield, 2024; Hanel et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This was unexpected given values theory and situated expectancy-value theory, which suggest that engaging in valued behaviors may motivate subsequent engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Hanel et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, previous tests of this mechanism using intensive longitudinal data have found that the importance of valued activities can predict subsequent behavioral engagement (Villanueva et al., 2020; Wieland et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Additionally, previous tests of this mechanism using intensive longitudinal data have found that the importance of valued activities can predict subsequent behavioral engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Villanueva et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Wieland et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, these studies examined prospective, goal-directed behaviors rather than whether the perceived value of completed behaviors predicts subsequent engagement.
Additioanlly, Villanueva et al., examined the relationship over a shorter time-scale.
text.formatted: Additioanlly, <ref type="bibr">Villanueva et al.,</ref> examined the relationship over a shorter time-scale.

text.text: In contrast, the present study assessed the perceived value of religious behaviors already performed, averaged across activities, and examined its association with total religious engagement the following day.
Thus, associations between perceived value and subsequent engagement may be behavior-specific or unfold over shorter intervals than those captured by daily assessments (Kuppens et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Thus, associations between perceived value and subsequent engagement may be behavior-specific or unfold over shorter intervals than those captured by daily assessments <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Kuppens et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Our fifth analysis found no credible evidence that perceived behavioral value moderated the within-person association between religious behavior duration and meaning in life (Figure 5, Table 5).
text.formatted: Our fifth analysis found no credible evidence that perceived behavioral value moderated the within-person association between religious behavior duration and meaning in life (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">5</ref>, Table <ref type="table">5</ref>).

text.text: This finding suggests that perceiving religious behaviors as more valuable does not reliably influence the relationship between how much time is spent engaging in religion and daily meaning in life.

This finding suggests that the duration of behavioral engagement and the perceived value of engaging in those behaviors may contribute independently to meaning in life rather than necessarily interacting.
Our sixth analysis was perhaps the most informative, revealing two distinct associations with meaning in life.

Although religious behavior duration and perceived value represent related dimensions of religious engagement, each appear to be independently associated with greater daily meaning, even after accounting for the other.
However, only perceived behavioral value was associated with meaning across individuals.

These findings extend prior research linking religiousness to meaning in life (Prinzing et al., 2023; Steger & Frazier, 2005) by demonstrating that time spent engaging in religious behaviors remains positively associated with daily meaning, even after accounting for their perceived value.
text.formatted: These findings extend prior research linking religiousness to meaning in life <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Prinzing et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Steger & Frazier, 2005)</ref> by demonstrating that time spent engaging in religious behaviors remains positively associated with daily meaning, even after accounting for their perceived value.

text.text: Furthermore, these findings extend the study of valued behaviors (Eccles & Wigfield, 2024; Maio, 2010) by demonstrating that perceived behavioral value was associated with meaning both within and between individuals, even after accounting for time spent engaging in those behaviors.
text.formatted: Furthermore, these findings extend the study of valued behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Maio, 2010)</ref> by demonstrating that perceived behavioral value was associated with meaning both within and between individuals, even after accounting for time spent engaging in those behaviors.

text.text: Together, these findings provide preliminary evidence that the time individuals spend engaging in religious behaviors and the value they place on those experiences may represent complementary but distinct pathways toward the development and maintenance of meaning in life.
The present study had several notable limitations.
First, the study had substantial missing data and excluded participants with insufficient repeated observations, potentially introducing selection bias.
However, missingness was primarily intermittent rather than due to dropout, and the remaining data made it possible to study repeated observations across a 50-day study period.
Second, low within-person reliability for perceived behavioral value and meaning in life may have influenced the associations and reduced the precision of our estimates.
Nevertheless, credible associations still emerged despite this which provides preliminary evidence for the relationships of interest.
Third, our primary findings were contemporaneous, preventing conclusions about temporal ordering or causality.
However, the intensive longitudinal design and RDSEM allowed us to still distinguish daily within-person associations from stable betweenperson differences while accounting for temporal dependencies.
Fourth, our sample consisted primarily of college students and was disproportionately female, White, and Latter-day Saint, potentially limiting generalizability to other populations.
However, participants were recruited across four universities and represented multiple religious affiliations, providing an initial foundation for replication in more diverse populations.
The present study identifies several promising directions for future research.

First, future studies should use more frequent assessments to examine whether associations between behavioral engagement, perceived behavioral value, and meaning in life unfold over shorter intervals, such as hours rather than days.
Second, future studies should investigate whether the perceived value of a specific behavior predicts subsequent engagement in that same behavior, rather than engagement across multiple behaviors.

Third, researchers should examine whether the independent associations of behavioral duration and perceived value with meaning in life extend to other developmental contexts in which individuals find meaning, such as relationships, education, or employment.

Finally, future studies should examine whether consistency in specific religious daily routines, rather than consistency in total time spent on religious behaviors day-to-day and week-to-week, predicts subsequent meaning in life.
The present study examined two potential pathways toward meaning in life: time spent engaging in religious behaviors and the perceived value of those behaviors.
Using intensive longitudinal data and residual dynamic structural equation modeling, we found that both duration and perceived value were independently associated with greater daily meaning in life.
These findings have implications for theory, research, and practice.

Theoretically, they suggest that simply perceiving a behavior as valuable, without necessarily identifying the underlying values or goals, may be relevant to meaning in life beyond behavioral engagement itself.

For research, these findings highlight the importance of considering not only how much individuals engage in behaviors, but also how much they value those experiences when studying the development and maintenance of meaning in life.
Finally, for practitioners, including clinicians and religious leaders, these findings suggest that encouraging religious engagement may be only part of the picture.
Helping individuals reflect on which religious experiences have been most valuable to them, and why, may offer another avenue for cultivating meaning in life.
Ultimately, the findings suggest that meaning in life may be associated not only with how much religion individuals practice, but also with how much those experiences matter to them.
